15              IV.     EPE’S ALLOCATION OF PRODUCTION COSTS

16   Q11. HOW DOES EPE CURRENTLY ALLOCATE ITS PRODUCTION-

17          RELATED COSTS?

18   A.     EPE’s Commission-approved 2 allocation of eligible production plant is to use the

19          4CP method to allocate its peaking generation facilities and to use the 4CP-A&E

20          method to allocate all other generation facilities. This does not apply to facilities
     2 Case No. 20-00104-UT

1            that are disallowed from New Mexico service like Newman Unit 6 and Palo

 2           Verde Unit 3 or any solar facilities that are direct assigned in the JCOS. 3

 3                  EPE allocates production O&M expenses based on whether the costs are

 4           demand- or energy-related. Demand-related production O&M is allocated using

 5           three primary demand allocators: D1PROD (4CP-A&E) for non-peaking

 6           generating facilities, battery capacity, and non-reconcilable purchased power;

 7           D2PROD (4CP) for peaking generating facilities; and DPROD12 (12CP-A&E)

 8           for year-round system control and dispatch expenses (FERC Account 556).

 9           Energy-related production O&M—covering expenses that vary with energy

10           output—is allocated using three energy allocators based on kWh at supply:

11           E1ENERGY (excluding non-firm kWh) for base-rate, non-fuel production O&M;

12           E1FUEL (including non-firm kWh) for reconcilable fuel and purchased power

13           recovered through the FPPCAC and RPS riders; and E2ENERGY (including non-

14           firm kWh) for non-reconcilable fuel-related items not recovered through riders

15           (such as fuel inventory, fuel-related Schedule M deferred tax items, or non-

16           demand imputed capacity/spinning reserves).

16   Q14. WHAT ARE DOD WITNESS LARRY BLANK’S REASONS FOR EPE TO

17        USE THE 4CP-A&E METHOD FOR ALL DEMAND PRODUCTION

18        COSTS?

19   A.   Dr. Larry Blank argues that a single demand production allocator would promote

20        consistency throughout EPE’s cost studies. He also points out that EPE witness

21        Victor Martinez states in his direct testimony that EPE operates its system as an


                                              10

                                    ADRIAN HERNANDEZ

1         integrated system so that goes against EPE wanting to use different allocation

2         treatment for peaking generation since even peaking generation resources support

3         the system’s broader demand requirement.       Dr. Blank also references EPE’s

4         recent Texas rate case where the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“PUCT”)

5         rejected the use of multiple demand production allocators in the class cost of

6         service study. Finally, Dr. Blank points out that the difference between using the

7         D1PROD (4CP-A&E allocator) and the D2PROD (4CP allocator) in the overall

 8        cost of service results is immaterial.

10   Q15. HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO DOD WITNESS LARRY BLANK’S

11        RECOMMENDATION THAT EPE USE THE 4CP-A&E METHOD

12        (D1PROD) FOR ALL DEMAND PRODUCTION COSTS?

13   A.   While applying a single production demand allocator (D1PROD) would certainly

14        be simpler, ease of administration should not override cost causation. EPE

15        proposes to continue using the 4CP allocator (D2PROD) for peaking generation

16        for two primary reasons.

17               First, it accurately reflects cost causation. As stated on page 38 of the

18        NARUC Electric Utility Cost Allocation Manual, "Cost causation is a phrase

19        referring to an attempt to determine what, or who, is causing costs to be incurred

20        by the utility. For the generation function, cost causation attempts to determine

21        what influences a utility's production plant investment decisions." Although EPE

 1          witness Martinez notes that EPE operates an integrated system, he also

 2          characterizes EPE’s generation fleet as a "diverse portfolio of resources," 4 and

 3          EPE witness Hughes details the distinct operational roles of those facilities. For

 4          example, Copper is unequivocally a peaking unit designed specifically to meet

 5          peak system demand, even though it operates within an integrated fleet.

 6          Allocating peaking plant on a 4CP basis directly aligns those capital costs with

 7          the jurisdictions and customer classes driving the need for peaking capacity.

 8                  Second, retaining the 4CP D2PROD allocator provides granular, peak-

 9          specific cost data that EPE witness Manuel Carrasco relies upon directly in his

10          rate design studies. 5 Abandoning the D2PROD allocator for simplicity’s sake

11          would sacrifice both cost-causation accuracy and valuable analytical inputs for

12          rate design.

11   A.     Staff witness Jester disagrees with EPE’s use of Maximum Class Demand

12          (“MCD”) to assign substation and primary distribution feeder costs and Non-

13          Coincident Peak Demand (“NCP”) to assign secondary voltage distribution

14          feeders and line transformer costs. Mr. Jester does not recommend changes in

15          this case, but for future rate cases he recommends the hourly cost method be used.

16                 DOD witness Blank raises an issue with EPE’s use of the NON-

17          AMS_METER allocator for non-AMS meter plant and the AMS_METER

18          allocator for AMS meter plant as well as the CUST902 allocator to allocate

 1   Q25. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO STAFF WITNESS JESTER?

 2   A.   EPE is open to examining alternative allocation methodologies in future filings,

 3        provided they accurately reflect cost causation. Shifting distribution allocations

 4        away from peak demand and toward energy usage ignores the primary drivers of

 5        EPE’s distribution capital investments—specifically, a growing residential

 6        population and the increasing penetration of refrigerated air conditioning, both of

 7        which directly drive localized peak demand. From a cost-allocation standpoint,

 8        peak demand remains the fundamental driver of distribution infrastructure costs.

 9

10   Q26. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO DOD WITNESS BLANK?

11   A.   Dr. Blank correctly identifies a disparity in the meter cost results. As I noted

12        earlier in my testimony, EPE updated the allocator used for the amortization of

13        legacy meters in its rebuttal CCOS study. Previously, EPE inadvertently applied

14        the NON-AMS allocator, which assigned legacy meter amortization to customer

15        classes incorrectly.   EPE corrected this error by applying the AMS_METER

16        allocator so that customers who received AMS meters bear the amortization costs

17        of the legacy meters those installations replaced. This correction substantially

18        alters the final meter cost results (classified under the CUST370 component) and

19        reduces the over-allocation of CUST370 costs to Rate Classes 10A, 10B, and 26

20        that Dr. Blank identified.
